newsitem.title: UK: UK PSBR data provide no grounds for big tax rises.
newsitem.headline: UK PSBR data provide no grounds for big tax rises.

text.p: A disappointing tax take pushed the UK's PSBR higher in May, but analysts said the long term trend shows the public finances are improving and provide little grounds for big tax rises in the budget.
The shortfall between government spending and tax receipts was 3.96 billion pounds in May compared with a deficit of 76 million pounds in April and a 3.22 billion pound deficit in May 1996.
"The disappointment came entirely on the receipts side, but those figures have been very erratic and are quite likely to bounce back next month," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
Any discouragement on the receipts side should be partly offset by the tight departmental spending in the month, he said.

"Departmental spending was one percent lower in May this year than the same month last year, which is three months in a row of negative year-on-year figures. That shows impressive restraint in expenditure continues."
Changes to the so-called 'payment on account' scheme for large VAT payers have led to a very erratic pattern of indirect tax receipts since the new rules were introduced last June.
The scheme allows large companies to pay only 1/24 of their VAT in the first two months of a three-month accounting period then settle the in the third month.

"Many large companies have chosen to pay the three-month balance in January, April, June and October which has made recepits much larger in those months than others," a spokesman for the Office for National Statistics said.

In May, for example, VAT receipts were 11.5 percent lower than May last year while April's take was up 40 percent on the year. But on a cumulative basis, VAT receipts for the fiscal year were up 11.1 percent year-on-year in May.

Cumulative total receipts were a little less impressive -- up only 4.5 percent -- but viewed on a six month basis they are running between six and seven percent higher than a year ago, well above the 5.0 percent growth factored in by current spending plans.
And cumulative PSBR figures are more impressive still.
"The finances remain on an improving trend. Taking both the April and May together the PSBR has narrowd by 35 percent compared to last year," said Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko.
However, economists said if the new government is looking for an excuse to raise taxes in theJuly 2 budget, it will find a way to use these data.

"No doubt this figure is going to be viewed as a justification of a change or abolition of advance corporation tax in the budget that has been talked about," said Kit Juckes, head of bond and currency strategy at NatWest Markets.
Speculation is building that the government will tighten fiscal policy by around 3.0 billion pounds in the budget, with the corporate sector and pension funds bearing the brunt of the tax rises.

And later this week, a report from the National Audit Office, commissioned by Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, is likely to present a rather gloomier medium term outlook for the public finances.
The government may seek to use this too as a justification for tax rises in July, analysts said.
